item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports combining individual sequences with global item transitions. [TGCL4SR (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28789) builds a temporal item-transition graph, combines graph convolution with a time-aware Transformer, and adds contrastive objectives. [LS4SRec (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3723173) uses a weighted global transition graph to supply collaborative signals for sparse sequences while separating long- and short-term interests. For explicit relation types, [KGSCL (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S089360802500070X) distinguishes substitution and complementarity through Amazon metadata relationships, using substitution for replacement augmentation and complementarity for insertion. Those relationship annotations are unavailable in this task; its reported gains do not establish that histories and text alone recover the same semantics.\n\nA feasible adaptation—an inference from these methods—is SASRec plus separate directed-transition and lexical-similarity channels, with a learned gate controlling their contributions. Build transitions exclusively from training histories; encode titles/descriptions using TF-IDF or randomly initialized pooled token embeddings trained with next-item prediction. Treat channels as behavioral succession and textual similarity: neither provides verified complement/substitute labels. Much recent text-based evidence depends on external pretrained representations; [WhitenRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10602), for example, explicitly uses pretrained text embeddings, so its gains cannot justify a scratch-trained encoder. The search found no directly verified 2024–2026 result establishing the complete proposed combination under these restrictions. Test transition-only, text-only, and gated combinations against SASRec using the pinned macro validation HR@10, with history-length breakdowns to assess sparse-user benefits."}
